title: Convention on Migratory Species
article: Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species of Wild Animals

definition.text: An international agreement, also called the Bonn Convention, to conserve migratory animals throughout their ranges.

facts.text: It was signed on 23 June 1979 in Bonn and took effect on 1 November 1983; its secretariat is run by UNEP.
Appendix I lists migratory species threatened with extinction, which range states must strictly protect.
Appendix II lists species that would benefit from international cooperation, the basis for regional or global agreements.
As a framework convention it has spawned seven agreements, such as one covering 254 wetland-dependent bird species, plus several memoranda of understanding.

definition.text: Genetic material from plants, animals, microbes or other sources that has actual or potential value.

facts.text: They are one of the three levels of biodiversity defined by the Biodiversity Convention in 1992.
Germplasm, for example, is genetic material kept for breeding, preservation and research.
Earlier agreements treated genetic resources as common heritage; the CBD instead gave each state sovereign rights over those in its territory.
Developing countries criticised the common heritage approach for letting their resources be exploited without compensation and commercialised in industrialised nations.

definition.text: The principle, from the Biodiversity Convention, that benefits from using genetic resources must be shared fairly with the country or community that provided them.

facts.text: Under the CBD, parties should ease access to genetic resources for environmentally sound uses and share research results and commercial benefits fairly.
The CBD's provisions were seen as too vague, leading to the non-binding Bonn Guidelines in 2002 and then the Nagoya Protocol.
The Nagoya Protocol requires prior informed consent and mutually agreed terms for access.
Benefits must be shared fairly with the providing party, including those from later applications and commercialisation.
Digital sequence data can be used without the physical material, escaping the bilateral access-based model.

title: Digital sequence information

definition.text: A placeholder policy term, used especially in the Biodiversity Convention, for data such as DNA sequences derived from genetic resources.

facts.text: It is crucial to research in public health, medicine, biodiversity, breeding and evolution.
Researchers share it freely online, which conflicts with benefit-sharing duties because users can access it without agreements.
At COP 15 in 2022 parties agreed a multilateral benefit-sharing mechanism that decouples access from benefit-sharing.
At COP 16 in 2024 they set up the Cali Fund, to which industries using DSI, such as pharma and cosmetics, are expected to contribute part of their profits.
Half of the Cali Fund is to go to local and Indigenous groups.

contested_note: The term itself remains disputed, and parties disagree over how open data should be reconciled with benefit-sharing.

title: High Seas Treaty

definition.text: A legally binding agreement under the Law of the Sea convention to conserve and sustainably use marine life in areas beyond national jurisdiction.

facts.text: Areas beyond national jurisdiction, the high seas and the international seabed, make up about two-thirds of the ocean and were largely unregulated.
The text was adopted on 19 June 2023; Morocco's ratification on 19 September 2025 made 60, and it took effect on 17 January 2026.
It covers four elements: marine genetic resources, area-based tools including marine protected areas, environmental impact assessments, and capacity building.
Benefits from marine genetic resources, used in cosmetics and medicines, are to be shared, both monetary and non-monetary; fish and fishing are excluded.
Marine protected areas on the high seas can be adopted by consensus or a three-quarter majority and then bind all parties.
Parties must carry out environmental impact assessments for activities that may affect the marine environment.
Negotiations turned on the tension between 'freedom of the seas' and 'common heritage of mankind'.

prerequisites: United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea
